units.title: Major Types of World Climates
units.intro:
Climate is the long-run mix of temperature and rainfall (plus wind, humidity). Weather is today’s sample. Classification in this book is mainly by heat and rain. Vegetation is the living stamp of that pair.

**Why climates sit where they sit:** latitude (sun angle), ITCZ and pressure belts, continent vs sea, ocean currents, altitude, rain-shadow mountains. Eritrea’s plateau is cooler than its latitude because of height — always say both.

cards.title: 1.1 Introduction to Climate
body: Climate is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period of time.
The word climate comes from the Greek klima, which means the inclination of the sun.
Climate is influenced by solar radiation and by the composition of the atmosphere.
Humans, in turn, can affect climate through changing the earth’s surface and releasing pollutants such as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
The goal of the geographical study of climate is to understand its distribution over the earth’s surface.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the world's climates is characterized by having the smallest annual temperature range, not exceeding 3 degrees Celsius?

steps.text: **Step 1: Check the thermal range of tropical climates.**
The Tropical Wet Climate has monthly temperatures close to $27^{\circ}\text{C}$ and an annual temperature range that does not exceed $3^{\circ}\text{C}$.
This is noted as the smallest annual range of temperature among all global climates.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the defining precipitation characteristic of the Mediterranean Climate?

options.A: Rainfall is concentrated entirely in summer, while winters are dry.
options.B: Abundant, uniform rainfall occurs throughout all months of the year.
options.C: Annual rainfall is concentrated entirely in winter, while summers are dry.
options.D: Precipitation falls almost entirely as winter snowfall.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall Mediterranean precipitation patterns.**
There are three distinctive characteristics of the Mediterranean Climate.

**Step 2: Identify the precipitation rule.**
Its annual rainfall is concentrated entirely in winter, while summers are almost completely rainless.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Annual rainfall is concentrated entirely in winter, while summers are dry.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The Tropical Wet Climate is located on both sides of the equator, extending generally between latitudes of:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Locate latitudinal parameters.i.**
The text states that the Tropical Wet Climate occurs on both sides of the equator.

**Step 2: Find the exact range.**
Its latitudinal range extends between $0^{\circ}\text{ to }5^{\circ}$ north and south of the equator.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct option is **0 degrees and 5 degrees N/S**.

cards.title: Tip
body: Name the climate, give a latitude or pressure reason, then name the plant belt. Three sentences beat a list of cities.

cards.title: Expanded notes
body: Tropical wet: high sun every month, convection rain most days, poor soils despite lush trees (nutrients live in the plants). Savanna: ITCZ visits then leaves — a wet season and a fire-dry season. Deserts: Sahara and Arabian sit under subtropical highs; coastal deserts can also sit by cold currents. Mediterranean: dry hot summer, wet winter — west coasts ~30–40°. Polar: low sun angle, albedo of ice.
Humans shift climate locally (city heat, deforestation) and globally (greenhouse gases). That sentence is the bridge to Unit 5 of Grade 11.

cards.title: Write climate as stacked causes
body: **Latitude:** high noon sun all year near the equator; slanted weak sun and long winter nights toward the poles.
**Pressure belts:** rising ITCZ = rain; sinking near 30° = many hot deserts. Winds then carry those air masses onto land.
**Sea vs land:** water changes temperature slowly, so coasts are milder and often wetter on the windward side. Interiors have huge ranges.
**Altitude:** about 6.5 °C cooler per 1000 m. A tropical-latitude plateau can farm like a temperate country. That is the Asmara sentence.
**Currents:** warm current + onshore wind = extra moisture; cold current = foggy coastal desert.
For Eritrea stack them: tropical latitude + Red Sea on the east + plateau height + dry descending or inland air in parts of the west. One-factor answers are too thin.

**Step 1: Recall the etymological origin of the word.**

**Step 2: Identify the literal translation.**

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The dense, coniferous forests of cold climates sweeping across northern Europe, Siberia, and Canada are collectively known as:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check high-latitude forest vocabulary.**
Think about the natural vegetation of cold climates.

**Step 2: Identify the term used in Russia/Siberia.**
Coniferous forest in northern Europe and Siberia is called Taiga.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct term is **Taiga**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The natural vegetation of cold climate is known as:
cards.why: **Taiga** (also known as boreal forest) consists of coniferous trees like pines and spruces. It is the characteristic vegetation of cold, subarctic climates found in northern regions like Siberia and Canada.

glossary.meaning: Climate is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period of time.

tips.text: Climate is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period of time. It has profound effects on vegetation and animal life, including humans.
Humans, in turn, can affect climate by changing the earth’s surface and by releasing chemicals such as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
The main aim of studying climate is to understand its distribution over the earth’s surface.
To understand the diversity of world climate better, the most important aspects must be selected and studied.
Temperature, precipitation and vegetation are widely used as bases for the classification of climate.

The classification of world climates is intended to be used as a useful learning tool. It helps to simplify and organize various types of climates into a system that helps us to understand the distribution and characteristics of each type.

questions.answer: Climate = long-term pattern. Weather = short-term state.
why: Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period (about 30 years); weather is the state of the atmosphere at a given time, which can change within hours.

questions.q: Why some west coasts are desert?
questions.answer: Cold current + sinking air / rain shadow (any valid pair).
why: On many west coasts in the tropics (Namib, Atacama) cold ocean currents cool the air so it cannot rise, and subtropical high pressure brings sinking dry air, so very little rain falls.

similar.q: A type of climate characterized mainly by clear skies and abundant sunshine is  A) Tropical Monsoon.  B) Tropical Savannah.  C) Tropical Desert.  D) Mediterranean.  E) West Margin.
similar.a: D. Mediterranean. — Hot deserts are also cloudless and sunny for most of the year (sub-tropical high pressure), so C is defensible on general knowledge. Monsoon, savannah and west-margin climates have cloudy rainy seasons. Answer: D (C also accepted).

questions.answer: Hot and dry.
why: In summer the subtropical high moves over Mediterranean regions, bringing sinking air, clear skies and drought; rain comes in the mild winter.

questions.q: Why is Asmara cooler than Massawa?
questions.answer: Altitude — same latitude family, different height.
why: Both cities are at about 15°N, but Asmara is about 2 300 m higher; temperature falls about 6.5 °C per 1 000 m, so Asmara is roughly 15 °C cooler.

questions.answer: Dry side of a mountain; air already dropped its rain on the windward slope.
why: Moist air rises and drops its rain on the windward slope; descending on the leeward side it warms and becomes drier, so that side receives little rain.

similar.q: Polar climates lack heat because?
similar.a: Low sun angle and long winters; ice reflects what little arrives.

questions.answer: Low sun angle and long winters; ice reflects what little arrives.
why: Near the poles the Sun is always low, so its energy is spread over a large area; winters have months of darkness, and snow and ice reflect much of the incoming radiation.

questions.answer: Dense evergreen rainforest.

questions.answer: Grassland with scattered trees.
why: The long dry season and frequent fires prevent dense forest, so savanna is tall grassland with scattered drought-resistant trees such as acacia and baobab.

questions.answer: Bigger temperature range inland; seas moderate coasts.
why: Land heats and cools faster than water, so places far inland have very hot summers and cold winters (large range), while coastal places have milder, more even temperatures.

questions.answer: Seasonal reversal of wind bringing a concentrated rainy season.
why: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds: in summer moist winds blow from the sea onto the heated land, bringing a heavy rainy season; in winter dry winds blow from the land.
